💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, following devastating hacks that caused European fridges to reach 50 degrees Celsius, destroying food stocks, the UK has implemented nationwide patching to ensure similar attacks won't affect its fridges.
  • Refrigeration consultants Omega Solutions were the first to identify the concern before the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), the Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs (Defra) and Food Standards Agency (FSA) all became involved in working on the problem.
  • Recent findings suggest that "From a business perspective, it could have been potentially devastating with business interruption and supply chain problems.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, following devastating hacks that caused European fridges to reach 50 degrees Celsius, destroying food stocks, the UK has implemented nationwide patching to ensure similar attacks won't affect its fridges. While it was thought that the UK had avoided similar hacks because it used different devices from those used in mainland Europe, an even worse issue was just waiting to be discovered. The BBC reports that a different flaw was discovered by security researchers in late October, one that could have caused even worse damage if it had been identified by hackers. Since then, work has been carried out to harden security across the U.K., with fridges in supermarkets, warehouses, and elsewhere now protected.

Refrigeration consultants Omega Solutions were the first to identify the concern before the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), the Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs (Defra) and Food Standards Agency (FSA) all became involved in working on the problem. As a precaution, thousands of devices that control tens of thousands of fridges were blocked from accessing the internet, with supermarket IT workers scrambling to sometimes physically isolate devices by removing network cables.

Recent findings suggest that "From a business perspective, it could have been potentially devastating with business interruption and supply chain problems. Our warehouses have millions of pounds worth of food that could have been spoiled if any hackers found out about this method of attack," one supermarket worker warned.

According to recent reports, the concern that they were trying to address rested within the most popular refrigeration controllers used across the U.K., made by British firm Resource Data Management (RDM). It was found that these controllers had a similar authentication security flaw to those hacked across Europe, although RDM points out that hacking its devices would have required a specific piece of hardware. However, that hardware is freely available.

RDM has since confirmed that there was no sign of any malicious activity on any of its controllers throughout the patching process.

In a recent development, the situation in France, Belgium, and other European countries was much more dire. After initially hitting France in October, a further wave of attacks swept through supermarkets and even blood banks. Even the fridges at a U.S. military base were not safe. While no responsibility for the attacks has been taken, France has so far laid the blame at the door of Iran — something the country's government denies.

Apple Intelligence, decoded: How to make sense of Apple’s confusing AI lineup

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2036 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Apple has received much criticism for being late to the AI game.
  • Sources indicate that apple has received much criticism for being late to the AI game.
  • Sources indicate that though the initial capabilities of Apple Intelligence were rather lackluster compared with its peers, Apple spent the next two years rapidly refining its offerings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple has received much criticism for being late to the AI game. While OpenAI helped define the AI boom beginning in late 2021, and Google and other tech giants rapidly jumped on the AI train the following year, Apple didn’t make its first real foray into artificial intelligence until 2024 with Apple Intelligence. Though the initial capabilities of Apple Intelligence were rather lackluster compared with its peers, Apple spent the next two years rapidly refining its offerings. In 2026, Apple made its AI system much more capable and expansive by introducing more advanced AI tools, including the Siri AI chatbot and Audio Intelligence. And just last month, Apple also debuted an additional AI tool dubbed “intelligent assistant.” The thing is, Apple now has so many AI offerings that it’s getting hard for the average consumer to keep track of what each one does, which devices support which AI tool, and which tools require a fee to access. So, here’s a cheat sheet for making sense of Apple’s increasingly confusing AI lineup. Apple Intelligence Apple Intelligence is the oldest of the manufacturer’s modern AI offerings, introduced in 2024. Think of Apple Intelligence as the foundational artificial intelligence layer integrated into Apple’s operating systems, including iOS, macOS, and watchOS. Apple Intelligence includes a suite of smaller AI tools tailored to specific tasks. For example, Apple Intelligence powers Visual Intelligence, which lets Apple’s AI see and understand what’s on your screen or through your camera and take action on it; for example, it can tell you the nutritional information of the food on your plate. Apple Intelligence powers Audio Intelligence, a tool that can help you identify sounds and music and even recap your spoken conversations on some Apple Watches. It is also the engine behind numerous other AI features across your Apple products, including image generation, live translation, select photo editing tools, message summaries, and more. Not every device that supports Apple Intelligence supports all its features. Any Mac with an Apple Silicon chip will run Apple Intelligence, but you’ll need a Mac with an M3 chip and 12 GB of RAM or more to use some of its most advanced features, including custom Siri Voices and advanced AI dictation. For the iPhone, you’ll need an iPhone 17 Pro or later to use those advanced Apple Intelligence features (iPhone 15 Pro and later is required for most Apple Intelligence features). As for Audio Intelligence on the Apple Watch, that’s limited to the newly introduced Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Series 4. Siri AI Siri AI is Apple’s new chatbot. Though people often use the terms “Siri AI” and “Apple Intelligence” interchangeably, they are actually distinct. Apple Intelligence is the foundational AI system integrated into Apple’s operating systems. Siri AI is the natural-language gateway to Apple Intelligence—it lets you communicate as you would with a person to give it commands or find information, which it then carries out using Apple Intelligence’s capabilities. Siri AI runs on the cloud on any device that supports iOS 27, macOS 27, iPadOS 27, visionOS 27, watchOS 27, and (soon) tvOS 27. However, if you want to run some aspects of Siri AI locally on your device, you’ll need a Mac with an M3 chip and 12GB of RAM or more, or an iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone Air, or later. Intelligent Assistant This is Apple’s newest major artificial intelligence tool, the most impressive, and the one that most muddies Apple’s AI branding. “Intelligent assistant,” introduced last month and released this month as part of the updated Logic Pro, Pages, Numbers, and Keynote apps in Apple’s paid Creator Studio suite, is a new natural-language AI tool aimed at helping creators be more productive. The tool is integrated into the above apps in the form of a chatbot. There’s a text field where you type instructions to the intelligent assistant (“make this piano track sound like it was recorded in a concert hall” or “fix the formula errors in this spreadsheet”). The changes happen like magic—all very impressive stuff. As a matter of fact, it’s way more impressive than the other capabilities Apple has shown off for Apple Intelligence and Siri AI. So why hasn’t Apple branded these new AI features as Apple Intelligence? The answer: Intelligent assistant is not powered by Apple Intelligence or Siri AI. Instead, the new AI tools use Apple Foundation Models combined with additional models from third-party providers, in this case, OpenAI and Google. This explains why intelligent assistant is so capable (both OpenAI and Google have a huge lead over Apple in the AI space) and also why Apple has eschewed the Apple Intelligence branding for the work it carries out. Does Apple charge for AI? This is where things get really muddied for people. Apple’s AI pricing runs from free, to a monthly subscription fee, to higher usage limits with select iCloud Plus intends. Currently, using Apple Intelligence and Siri AI is free for all consumers. However, Apple claims this won’t last. With the release of the 27.3 versions of its operating systems in December, customers will have daily limits when using Siri AI and Apple Intelligence. If they exceed those limits, they won’t be able to use any Apple Intelligence features that require cloud processing (which costs Apple compute power). If users do want higher Apple Intelligence and Siri AI limits, they can get more by paying for an iCloud Plus plan (if they don’t already have one). The 50GB iCloud Plus plan, which costs just 99 cents per month, doesn’t increase your AI limits. However, the other iCloud Plus plans do: 200GB ($2.99 per month): 2x limit increase 2TB ($9.99 per month): 5x limit increase 6TB ($29.99 per month): 10x limit increase 12TB ($59.99 per month): 20x limit increase As for intelligent assistant access in Logic Pro, Pages, Keynote, and Numbers, users already need to pony up. Intelligent assistant is available only as part of Apple’s Creator Studio subscription bundle, for which it charges $12.99 per month or $129 per year. This means that if you want as much access as possible to Apple’s AI offerings, you’ll need to subscribe to two subscription plans.

Roborock has launched its Black Friday 2026 deals with some killer discounts including up to half off select models, and over $1650 off its flagship offering.

Starting on November 19 and through the end of this month, you can score deals on select Roborock products including some of the brand’s best robot vacuums.

That starts with the current Roborock flagship, the Saros 20. This robot vacuum includes the best navigation and cleaning tech, all wrapped up in a package that’s easy to use and, at Black Friday, a great deal.

Saros 20 includes Roborock’s StarSight Autonomous System 2.0 to navigate around your home safely and avoid obstacles, combining that with the AdaptiLift Chassis 3.0 which can raise the robot up over double-layer steps up to 3.46-inches in height – room dividers, trim, and more are a breeze for this one. Plus, the robot’s thin 3.13-inch profile means it can fit under many furniture items for a deeper clean. The vacuum measures in at 36,000 Pa of suction power while employing a Dual anti-tangle system for eliminating hair tangles on the brush. The built-in mop scrubs the floor while also being able to reach into corners, and when it’s time to head back to the dock, the dustbin auto-empties while heated water and air clean and dry the mops.

For Black Friday 2026, Roborock Saros 20 is discounted to $989.99, down 38% ($610) from its retail price of $1,599.99. It’s the lowest price ever on the robot.

The Roborocok Qrevo Edge 3 Pro offers many of the same benefits, but at a slightly lower price.

In a recent development, thin profile, AdaptiLift Chassis 3.0, DuoDivide brush, 36,000 Pa of suction power, 300+ object recognition, and an auto-empty/auto-clean dock, Qrevo Edge 3 Pro is packed with many of the same features and functions as Saros 20. The key differences with this model include the use of a warm-water mopping system that applies downward pressure for cleaning your floors, as well as a different design, and a more affordable price tag.

Qrevo Edge 3 Pro is 40% off for Black Friday, cutting its price down to $899.99.

Offering one of the best values in a robot vacuum under $400, the Roborock Qrevo S Pro offers up powerful 18,500 Pa suction, a built-in dual-brush mop, an auto-empty/auto-clean dock using heated water and air, and more.

And it’s just $379.99 for Black Friday.

This is one of the best values you’ll find in a robot vacuum this holiday season, so don’t miss it!

Robot vacuums are great, but sometimes a manual touch is key. That’s where the Roborock F25 Steam and F25 XT come into the picture.

The Roborock F25 Steam is a cordless wet/dry vacuum and mop that includes 25,000 Pa of suction power along with 356°F VaporFlow Steam so you can clean up even tough messes without harsh chemicals. It has a 1,000 ml water tank on board and up to 80 minutes of cleaning time on a charge, and it self-cleans when docked using high-temp washing and drying. F25 Steam is 42% off for Black Friday, down to $349.99.

In a recent development, roborock F25 XT, meanwhile, features 20,000 Pa suction power as well as both a dual-scraper system for its mop and automatic dispensing of cleaning solutions based on dirt levels, making it easy to clean up your floors. F25 XT is 57% off, down to $234.99.

Some other notable deals in Robrock’s Black Friday sale include the Roborock Qrevo 2 Pro, powerful package that makes for a major upgrade to your existing robot vacuum at $449.99, as well as the Roborock Q10 S5+, which packs powerful suction and an auto-empty dock for just $229.99 on Black Friday.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that want more housing market stories from Lance Lambert’s ResiClub in your inbox? Subscribe to the ResiClub newsletter. Based on ResiClub’s analysis of the Zillow Home Value Index, nationally aggregated U.S. home prices rose 0.7% year over year from October 2025 to October 2026. That marks another month-over-month deceleration, down from the 1.0% year-over-year increase from September 2025 to September 2026 and the 1.3% year-over-year increase from August 2025 to August 2026. After contracting over the past year, the number of America’s major regional housing markets seeing year-over-year declines is rising again, as the already soft national housing market (which is still amid the multiyear post-boom cyclical cooling window) sees another burst of softening amid the recent run-up in long-term yields and mortgage rates. —> 54 of the nation’s 300 largest housing markets (i.e., 18% of markets) had a falling year-over-year home price reading in the August 2025 to August 2026 window. —> 66 of the nation’s 300 largest housing markets (i.e., 22% of markets) had a falling year-over-year home price reading in the September 2025 to September 2026 window. —> 76 of the nation’s 300 largest housing markets (i.e., 25% of markets) had a falling year-over-year home price reading in the October 2025 to October 2026 window. We should point out that the nationally aggregated housing market is softer than the counts above suggest, given that year-over-year home price declines are presently skewed slightly toward larger metro areas. Home prices are still climbing a tad nominally (not inflation-adjusted) year over year in some pockets where active inventory remains well below pre-pandemic 2019 levels, such as certain areas in the Northeast and Midwest. In contrast, some pockets in states like Texas, Florida, Washington, and Colorado—where active inventory exceeds pre-pandemic 2019 levels by a solid clip—are seeing either material corrections, modest home price pullbacks, or simply flat pricing. Looking ahead, the big question is how much of a burst of softening the nationally aggregated housing market will see, now that the 30-year fixed-mortgage rate has jumped back above 7.0% amid an already strained affordability environment and the still ongoing post-boom cyclical cooling period. To keep an eye on it, ResiClub recommends closely monitoring local active inventory/months of supply over the next several months. Click here for an interactive version of the chart below. Many of the housing markets seeing the most softness, where homebuyers have gained the most leverage since the pandemic housing boom fizzled out, are primarily located in Sunbelt regions or the Mountain West. Many of these areas saw even greater price surges during the pandemic housing boom, with home price growth outpacing local income levels. As pandemic-driven domestic migration slowed and mortgage rates rose in 2022, markets like Tampa, Florida, and Austin faced challenges, relying on local income levels to support frothy home prices. That Sunbelt softening was further compounded by an abundance of fresh-home supply in the Sunbelt. Builders are often willing to lower prices or offer affordability incentives to maintain sales, which also has a cooling effect on the resale market. As a result, some buyers who might have previously opted for existing homes are instead choosing new construction with more attractive deals—which added further upward pressure to resale inventory growth over the past few years. Of course, while 76 of the nation’s 300 largest metro-area housing markets are seeing year-over-year home price declines, another 224 are seeing year-over-year home price increases. However, most of the places posting “nominal gains” are seeing gains below income growth and consumer price growth, which economists call “real” (inflation-adjusted) home price declines. Where are home prices still up on a year-over-year basis? See the map below. Below is a historical chart showing the year-over-year change in home prices across the 50 largest metro housing markets, with the yellow line representing the national aggregate, dating back to 2000. While the range [see chart above] between the strongest and weakest metro-area housing markets right now is fairly normal historically speaking, the bifurcation (i.e., direction) itself—the share of markets with rising home prices versus those with falling prices—is wider than normal, given that national appreciation is in a softer market with growth barely above 0.0%. And the longer some markets remain in the “rising” camp while others stay in the “falling” camp, the wider the gulf can become between the relatively more resilient markets and the weaker ones. For example, home prices in the Hartford, Conneticut, metro area are now 28.0% above their 2022 peak, while home prices in the Austin metro area sit 28.8% below their 2022 peak. Some of that bifurcation boils down to mean reversion, with many of the outright home price declines occurring in markets that overheated further during the pandemic housing boom. Note: For the historical chart below, we analyzed the 200 largest markets rather than the 300 used above, as some markets ranked 201 to 300 lack complete data going back to 2000. When weighted by population (not visualized), the housing market appears slightly weaker than the chart below suggests—which aligns with the fact that among just the 50 largest housing markets, 21 (42%) are currently posting negative year-over-year price growth, and nationally aggregated home prices are up just 0.7% year over year using the Zillow Home Value Index.

AI features could be turned off with a simple toggle, Canva proves

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that AI has taken over everything in the past few years, with AI features bombarding virtually every app or service available.
  • Canva today declared “AI Controls,” a new toggle that completely turns off generative AI features within the editing app.
  • In a recent development, generative AI can be quite helpful in working on posters, editing images, and more, but it’s not everyone’s preference.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that AI has taken over everything in the past few years, with AI features bombarding virtually every app or service available. If you’ve ever wanted to just turn off AI features, Canva proves that it could be a simple toggle, if companies actually wanted to give you a choice.

Canva today declared “AI Controls,” a new toggle that completely turns off generative AI features within the editing app.

In a recent development, generative AI can be quite helpful in working on posters, editing images, and more, but it’s not everyone’s preference. Canva puts this well:.

Recent findings suggest that for some people, AI is the most exciting creative tool in a generation, while others prefer bringing their ideas to life without it. We believe the future of creativity should give everyone the freedom to choose their own path, whether that’s creating with AI, without it, or somewhere in between.

Sources indicate that to give its users the choice, Canva’s Permissions menu now has a simple toggle for “Enable Generative AI features.” Toggling it off disables features such as Magic Write and Magic Edit. There’s also an option to limit how much AI-generated imagery appears in the Canva library.

Put simply, this is great to see.

AI has its place, but everyone should have a choice like this, especially when it comes to apps and services used for artistry in the same vein as Canva. Yet, the tech industry continues to go in the opposite direction, shoving AI into every corner whether it’s actually useful or not. Canva proves, though, that it doesn’t have to be that way.

#69998. Latest Update: Phison details SSD with a built-in NPU and 64GB of memory that supports AI frameworks on the drive

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1852 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomshardware ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Phison details SSD with a built-in NPU and 64GB of memory that supports AI frameworks on the drive

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1852 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Phison detailed two new enterprise SSD designs at Supercomputer 2026 (SC26) that aim to answer two separate problems: one with a built-in NPU and 64GB of 130 GB/s memory that supports running PyTorch, vLLM, OpenVINO, and llama.cpp directly on the drive, and another that merges fast pSLC cache with large QLC capacity behind just one controller.
  • Recent findings suggest that the computational-storage design’s premise is that a server can offload more to the SSD, which runs AI code on the data where it already resides and sends back results, instead of whole datasets.
  • Phison says that the integrated NPU is expected to deliver “36,800 DMIPS of compute performance,” or Dhrystone Million Instructions Per Second, a typical synthetic benchmark.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Phison detailed two new enterprise SSD designs at Supercomputer 2026 (SC26) that aim to answer two separate problems: one with a built-in NPU and 64GB of 130 GB/s memory that supports running PyTorch, vLLM, OpenVINO, and llama.cpp directly on the drive, and another that merges fast pSLC cache with large QLC capacity behind just one controller. The tech giant notes that “many of the products and features mentioned are still in development” and will arrive once finalized.

Recent findings suggest that the computational-storage design’s premise is that a server can offload more to the SSD, which runs AI code on the data where it already resides and sends back results, instead of whole datasets. The pSLC-QLC design, meanwhile, puts the cache inside each drive, which may reduce system complexity, as every drive bay contributes usable capacity and none goes to dedicated cache drives.

Phison says that the integrated NPU is expected to deliver “36,800 DMIPS of compute performance,” or Dhrystone Million Instructions Per Second, a typical synthetic benchmark. This is admittedly an old CPU integer benchmark from the 1980s, while NPUs tend to be rated in TOPS, but that figure was not given. For reference, the Topaz NPU add-in card Phison indicated at Computex carried eight NPUs rated at up to 40 TOPS each. The DMIPS figure therefore likely refers to, instead, the CPU cores that work alongside it, which we would expect to be based on an Arm Cortex design, adequate for running an SSD of this class but no measure of its AI capability.

In a recent development, the memory and its bandwidth are more crucial for the expected workload, anyway, and while the manufacturer doesn’t state the type, LPDDR5X is a popular option and may be used with the Topaz NPU, according to one secondary report. If the drive is a PCIe 6.0 part comparable to Phison’s X3 controller, it could hit up to 28 GB/s to the host, which would put the memory above 4x that speed. For reference, 130 GB/s is a bit less than half of that of the DGX Spark’s hardware, designed for AI development.

It has been revealed that phison claims developers can build on the drive “without specialized programming tools,” which, in this case, is a good thing. The drive does, of course, support multiple general-purpose inference servers and runtimes, but nothing was disclosed about how a host reaches the drive’s compute. The drives “scan and process data in parallel,” which indicates scalability, and return “relevant results” which Phison claims could mean 10 to 100 times less data transferred for applicable workloads. This may free up the host CPU for other tasks.

Phison’s idea to put compute on storage isn’t new. Samsung tried this with its SmartSSD — where an FPGA sat on the drive to process data without moving it — which was shown in 2018. Later, in 2022, the design was refined with AMD’s Xilinx Versal FPGA in its second generation, with Samsung claiming more than 50% lower processing time, up to 70% lower energy consumption, and up to 97% lower server CPU usage for scan-heavy database queries, compared to conventional SSDs. The drive has reportedly since disappeared from Samsung’s lineup, though the first-generation model was still sold under AMD’s Xilinx name as of last year.

It has been revealed that scaleFlux took a narrower route, with compression handled inside the SSD controller. The server doesn’t see this, so the drive looks like any other NVMe SSD, and no application has to change its behavior. The CEO claims it is the only organization with computational storage in production at hyperscalers. This suggests that not making customers write new code for the drive is the secret to success, as SmartSSD needed that for its FPGA and for each workload. Phison’s selling point here is flexibility for the client to use code written for common AI frameworks.

Firm CTO Sebastien Jean, writing in All About Circuits in 2025, argued that generic computational storage had stalled because “each use case is highly unique and it’s simply not scalable.” He called the idea of running the Linux operating system on a drive with bigger processors a “pie-in-the-sky approach.”.

It has been revealed that accelerators have long been widely used in data centers, and Jean’s proposal was to put targeted ones inside the SSD, each running a set operation over a range of logical block addresses (LBAs). By his reckoning, a chassis with 90 PCIe 6.0 SSDs could process data at 2.5 TB/s without affecting the CPU. The design revealed at SC26, though, appears closer to the general-purpose model, possibly due to the increasing relevance of AI and the demand for both memory and compute.

Jean also spoke at the Emerging Storage Technology panel at the conference to discuss future developments, including PCIe 7.0 drives that would operate at “50, 56 gigabytes per second,” which he called “faster than a DDR channel.” With 32 drives at this speed, a single chassis could reach “1.8 terabytes per second.” He described this specifically as computational storage for HPC.

Turning to the Mixed Media solution, that’s the “high-endurance pSLC and high-capacity QLC flash” SSD; it’s a 16-channel part, so not comparable to anything you see in retail. The pSLC portion of the drive has the 4-bit QLC flash act in a 1-bit SLC mode, which trades space for performance and endurance. Phison states the design builds on standard NVMe interfaces and fits into existing infrastructure “without requiring specialized host software.”.

Jean elaborated at the same panel that the “endurance group on the drive, which is SLC,” is managed separately from the XLC — 3-bit TLC or 4-bit QLC — and each region gets a namespace, so it appears as multiple drives to the OS. Then, high-write data can be sent specifically to the SLC group, while data in the QLC is likely to be more read-heavy. This follows a general trend of enterprise shifting toward QLC for capacity, but having some of it in SLC mode can help reduce the need for specialized caching.

In a recent development, right now, high-capacity SSDs usually have separate SSDs to fulfill this role, but that takes up more drive bays. The tradeoff with Phison’s approach is that a single drive failure takes out both capacity and a share of the cache. That said, Phison’s approach is more robust from a cache perspective, as “losing one drive out of 24 would result in a 4% cache loss instead of a 25% loss,” the firm says, with the 25% presumably assuming four dedicated cache drives.

Dedicated cache drives need tiering handled by the host or array software, while with Mixed Media each drive holds both tiers and the host simply picks the namespace it wants to write to.

The tech giant is not the first to have this idea, either, as Kioxia presented its Mixed Mode idea during FMS 2025, where each drive has a ratio of pSLC to QLC, set once per drive when it’s first used. Kioxia called 1:4 a “good beginning ratio,” though it remarked customers typically want pSLC at just 0.5% to 2% of maximum QLC capacity. That implementation also had parity protection on the pSLC space across multiple drives. Kioxia similarly marketed the benefit of needing fewer slots and field-replaceable units (FRUs), and its slides even used the term “Mixed Media” in two chart headings.

It has been revealed that dapuStor went further with its dual-mode J5060, a QLC SSD with a pSLC region that was in customer validation as of August; it compared the design against “four dedicated SLC drives” in a 24-drive system, the kind of setup that would produce Phison’s 25% figure. Solidigm’s Cloud Storage Acceleration Layer works differently, with a host-side flash translation layer, where it can manage small writes on SLC or TLC drives before writing to QLC in favorable large sequential chunks.

Recent findings suggest that there’s also the Enmotus FuzeDrive P200, previewed at CES 2020 as the MiDrive, which used a Phison controller and seems to be the closest to an ancestor of the current Mixed Media. That consumer drive, which we reviewed in 2021, had SLC and QLC portions that acted distinctly, but they were managed by Enmotus software.

In every drive, behind one 16-channel controller.

Separate NVMe endurance groups assigned to namespaces; no specialized host software, Phison says.

In every drive, with parity protection on the pSLC space across drives.

1:4 as a “good beginning ratio”; customers typically want pSLC at 0.5% to 2% of maximum QLC capacity.

Ratio set once, creating a pSLC namespace and endurance group.

In every drive, as a pSLC region beside the QLC.

400GB, 800GB or 1.2TB of pSLC on a 30.72TB drive.

Separate SLC and QLC block devices on one drive.

In the drive, as a fixed SLC portion of a consumer QLC SSD.

On dedicated SLC or TLC cache drives.

Reference system: three 800GB SLC drives and seven 61.44TB QLC drives.

Flash translation layer running on the host.

According to recent reports, it’s also inevitable that these two approaches will be compared to Phison’s other upcoming part, the X3 enterprise SSD controller, a PCIe 6.0 design promising up to 28 GB/s of sequential throughput and 6.8 million IOPS. Those figures are unchanged since Computex in June.

Recent findings suggest that the X3’s IOPS sounds like a lot, but we’ve heard considerable banter about AI needing way more than that, as Nvidia’s roadmap target for PCIe 7.0 is at 100 million IOPS, though that target counts 512-byte reads, a smaller unit than the 4KB that SSD ratings usually use, so the two figures aren’t directly comparable. Jean remarked at the panel that Phison is “very optimistic” it can achieve that. He added that the eightfold jump in IOPS that comes with moving from 4KB to 512-byte accesses would, on existing NAND, mean “eight times as much power,” or “roughly in the 140 to 180 watt range,” which is beyond reasonable, so perhaps a different solution will be required.

For the X3, Phison told us in June to expect customer samples by the end of the year, with volume coming in the middle of next year, though the SC26 release gives no dates. Notably, Micron and Samsung are already offering PCIe 6.0 SSDs, and the Bravera SC6 controller is expected from Marvell. Phison also says its PS7161, which its site lists as a customer sample, is “the first PCIe 6.0 redriver on the PCI-SIG Integrators List.”.

Industry observers note that of the two designs, Mixed Media looks like the nearer product. It builds on standard NVMe features, and DapuStor’s similar dual-mode drive reached customer testing this summer, while the one processor figure given for the computational-storage drive says little about what it can do for AI. What remains to be seen for Mixed Media is its pSLC-to-QLC ratio and how configurable it is. CES and Computex are the notable dates on the 2027 calendar to find out more about both, as well as the X3.

Shane Downing is a Contributing Writer for Tom’s Hardware, covering consumer storage, PC hardware, and AI.

Canva added an AI ‘kill switch’ to its tools

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1507 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that over the last few years, Canva, the Australian design platform, has been stuffing generative AI into its products.
  • Sources indicate that over the last few years, Canva, the Australian design platform, has been stuffing generative AI into its products.
  • Recent findings suggest that the first button seems like pure theater to me.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that over the last few years, Canva, the Australian design platform, has been stuffing generative AI into its products. Now, it’s giving you the option to make those AI features disappear. On Thursday, the manufacturer declared two newly introduced switches to rein in its AI for anyone on Canva Free and Canva Pro. One toggle button hides its generative AI features. Another one will make Canva show less AI-generated material in its library of templates and graphics. The first button seems like pure theater to me. If a user doesn’t want to use AI tools, it’s easy enough to figure out how: Don’t press the sparkly AI button. The second one is more useful, however, since it can help users avoid being drowned by AI-generated material while browsing the Canva libraries that made this suite popular in the first place. It’s worth noting that the switch doesn’t ban all AI-generated material from view—it just shows less. [Image: Canva] Both switches are buried in two settings menus. The general AI “kill switch” lives under Profile > Settings > Permissions. Flip it off, and Canva’s generative features are “hidden across Canva,” the company said in an announcement. These include Magic Expand, which extends a photo, and Canva Craft, the first generative image model developed by the company. You can turn them back on whenever you like. Still, Canva hasn’t erased every AI thingamajig. The suite’s AI-based Background Remover and Magic Grab—which picks an object out of a picture to move it somewhere else in the design—are “assistive editing tools,” and therefore are still accessed after toggling AI off. The second control sits under Profile > Your Account > AI Personalization (more on this later). Turn it on, and Canva cuts back the AI-generated material that pops up in search results and recommendations, pushing more human-made stuff to the top. The company says its AI content is only “a small portion” of its library, like abstract backgrounds and illustrated graphics. [Image: Canva] Why, really The filter matters to people who don’t want to wade through a river full of generative AI creations. It also benefits the humans behind the designs. Canva pays actual humans each time someone uses their work in a design. In theory, that steers money toward the designers and illustrators who fill the Canva library. These features are essentially a temperature check on AI. Players are coming to ‘GTA VI’ for the car chases, but staying for the wildlife

💡 Key Takeaways

  • After a 13-year wait, Rockstar Games’s Grand Theft Auto VI has been released—but for many players, a life of crime isn’t the only appeal.
  • The game is set in Leonida (Florida, but fictionalized), and outside Vice City’s limits, the state’s characteristic swamps, waters, and subtropical forests sprawl across the map.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that after a 13-year wait, Rockstar Games’s Grand Theft Auto VI has been released—but for many players, a life of crime isn’t the only appeal. The game is set in Leonida (Florida, but fictionalized), and outside Vice City’s limits, the state’s characteristic swamps, waters, and subtropical forests sprawl across the map. Expansive, painstakingly rendered landscapes have long been an integral part of Rockstar’s open-world action-adventure games, including its last major release, Red Dead Redemption 2. As in that title, in GTA VI, the natural world is more than just a backdrop for the main story: Side quests like alligator hunting and a zoologist challenge lead players into the great outdoors. Players have eagerly anticipated the wildlife. A promotional image featuring a lionfish—an invasive species in Florida—sparked hopeful discussion about spear hunting, which is one of the methods used to control their population. Other fans kept running lists of species confirmed ahead of the release date. GTA VI’s birding gameplay and inclusion of 62 avian species has been a particular source of buzz online, and hobbyists are already logging the species they spy on a dedicated website called Leonida Birds. One person noted that playing Red Dead Redemption 2 had “flipped the birding switch on,” and that they’ve since identified birds from the game in real life. Perhaps unsurprisingly, research suggests that this deep immersion in video game environments can serve as a valuable way to communicate information about the real natural world, including a study in which RDR2 players correctly identified more photos of wildlife species that had appeared in the game than non-players. “Not sure how GTA VI has suddenly turned me into David Attenborough,” one player remarked on X, “but I just logged off an 8 hour session and immediately want to hop back on to study more birds and wildlife.” In a study published in Geoscience Communication this week, researchers used GTA V’s digital replication of Los Angeles—coupled with data like Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change projections and records of past flooding—to simulate floods caused by sea level rise. Paul Nörenberg, one of the researchers, said in a press release that engaging with these climate effects in a familiar landscape “can bridge a gap in a way that conventional visualizations, such as models or maps, struggle to achieve.” Another study, which interviewed gamers about their experiences, observed that different games allow participants to explore nature through different contexts and perspectives, and games that include environmental destruction “made them contend with exploiting and subjugating nature—both in-game and in the actual world.” Though Grand Theft Auto’s plots are designed to let players explore a life of crime—not climate disaster—the fresh installment’s gameplay does weave in a range of real-world environmental topics, from animal conservation to chemicals in agriculture. One mission centers on the exotic animal trade; another involves freeing an orca from the Vice City Oceanarium, likely a reference to the now-shuttered Miami Seaquarium, which faced criticism for owning an orca named Lolita that died in captivity in 2023. In a third, a strawberry grower asks the player to visit a meth lab to pick up “discontinued” chemicals that he sprays on his unnaturally large crops, according to an IGN walk-through. This also echoes reality. Driscoll’s, a major agribusiness, faces a class-action lawsuit that alleges the organization sold strawberries contaminated with harmful chemicals without disclosing them. Video game realism does have its limits: The real-life strawberries haven’t turned anyone into giant mutants. Yet.

After a 13-year wait, Rockstar Games’s Grand Theft Auto VI has been released—but for many players, a life of crime isn’t the only appeal.

The game is set in Leonida (Florida, but fictionalized), and outside Vice City’s limits, the state’s characteristic swamps, waters, and subtropical forests sprawl across the map.

Recent findings suggest that expansive, painstakingly rendered landscapes have long been an integral part of Rockstar’s open-world action-adventure games, including its last major release, Red Dead Redemption 2. As in that title, in GTA VI, the natural world is more than just a backdrop for the main story: Side quests like alligator hunting and a zoologist challenge lead players into the great outdoors.

Industry observers note that players have eagerly anticipated the wildlife. A promotional image featuring a lionfish—an invasive species in Florida—sparked hopeful discussion about spear hunting, which is one of the methods used to control their population. Other fans kept running lists of species confirmed ahead of the release date.

GTA VI’s birding gameplay and inclusion of 62 avian species has been a particular source of buzz online, and hobbyists are already logging the species they spy on a dedicated website called Leonida Birds. One person stated that playing Red Dead Redemption 2 had “flipped the birding switch on,” and that they’ve since identified birds from the game in real life.

Perhaps unsurprisingly, research suggests that this deep immersion in video game environments can serve as a valuable way to communicate information about the real natural world, including a study in which RDR2 players correctly identified more photos of wildlife species that had appeared in the game than non-players.

“Not sure how GTA VI has suddenly turned me into David Attenborough,” one player remarked on X, “but I just logged off an 8 hour session and immediately want to hop back on to study more birds and wildlife.”.

In a study published in Geoscience Communication this week, researchers used GTA V’s digital replication of Los Angeles—coupled with data like Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change projections and records of past flooding—to simulate floods caused by sea level rise.

Paul Nörenberg, one of the researchers, remarked in a press release that engaging with these climate effects in a familiar landscape “can bridge a gap in a way that conventional visualizations, such as models or maps, struggle to achieve.”.

Another study, which interviewed gamers about their experiences, observed that different games allow participants to explore nature through different contexts and perspectives, and games that include environmental destruction “made them contend with exploiting and subjugating nature—both in-game and in the actual world.”.

Though Grand Theft Auto’s plots are designed to let players explore a life of crime—not climate disaster—the new installment’s gameplay does weave in a range of real-world environmental topics, from animal conservation to chemicals in agriculture.

One mission centers on the exotic animal trade; another involves freeing an orca from the Vice City Oceanarium, likely a reference to the now-shuttered Miami Seaquarium, which faced criticism for owning an orca named Lolita that died in captivity in 2023.

In a third, a strawberry grower asks the player to visit a meth lab to pick up “discontinued” chemicals that he sprays on his unnaturally large crops, according to an IGN walk-through. This also echoes reality. Driscoll’s, a major agribusiness, faces a class-action lawsuit that alleges the manufacturer sold strawberries contaminated with harmful chemicals without disclosing them.

Recent findings suggest that video game realism does have its limits: The real-life strawberries haven’t turned anyone into giant mutants. Yet.

Recent findings suggest that there’s a familiar interruption that comes with shopping online: you’ve found what you want, you’re ready to check out, and the store asks you to sign in. Was this the account with your usual password? Did you change it last time? Is it easier to reset it again?

Recent findings suggest that for Black Friday, Proton Pass Plus and Pass Family are both 60% off their regular monthly pricing with a one-year subscription, while Proton Unlimited is 50% off. Pass Plus starts at $1.99 per month, billed annually, making this a good opportunity to get your passwords — and a few other key parts of your digital life — organized.

The problem with strong passwords isn’t understanding why you need them; it’s keeping track of a different one for every account.

That’s useful whether you’re creating an account for a single purchase or signing into a service you use every day.

Unique passwords also help limit the fallout from a data breach. If a retailer exposes your login credentials, using a different password elsewhere means those same credentials won’t unlock your other accounts.

With unlimited logins and encrypted vaults that sync across devices, Proton Pass lets you keep those details together as you move between your phone and computer.

It has been revealed that proton Pass is available for practically every platform, from Chrome and Firefox on the web to native macOS, Windows, and Linux apps to, of course, iOS and Android. This makes it trivially easy to access your passwords, passkeys, and API credentials wherever you find yourself.

Black Friday shopping often leaves something behind long after the packages arrive: a steady stream of promotional emails from stores you barely remember visiting.

Proton Pass includes unlimited hide-my-email aliases, giving you an alternative to handing out your real address every time you create an account.

Recent findings suggest that an alias is an extra email address that forwards messages to your normal inbox. You can give it to a shopping website and still receive your order confirmations and delivery updates, without sharing the underlying address you use for everything else.

If that alias starts receiving spam, you can switch it off. Your real email address stays the same, and you don’t have to patch all your other accounts.

It’s a practical way to put some distance between your primary inbox and the websites you’re trying for the first time. A separate alias for each service also gives you more control: you can stop messages arriving through one address without disrupting the others.

Passwords are only part of what’s worth keeping in a secure, accessible place.

Industry observers note that proton Pass also stores notes, credit card details, and other confidential information in end-to-end encrypted vaults. That makes it useful for the small, everyday moments when you need something sensitive and don’t want to go looking for it.

When you’re booking a flight, saved passport details let you look up the information you need without digging through a drawer halfway through the reservation.

When you’re shopping online, saved card details mean you don’t have to leave the checkout page to find your wallet.

In a recent development, when you’re traveling, keeping a digital copy of an important document within reach gives you a convenient reference while you’re away from home. It doesn’t replace an original document where one is required, but it can save you from searching through scattered files and messages.

Pass Plus also includes a built-in two-factor authenticator, Dark Web Monitoring, and secure link and vault sharing. Those features give you more ways to manage access to your accounts and share sensitive information when you need to.

Pass Plus is the straightforward choice for one person who wants password generation, autofill, unlimited aliases, and secure storage.

Pass Family includes six Pass Plus accounts and a family admin panel. If several people in your household need a password manager, it’s worth considering rather than setting everyone up with separate subscriptions.

According to recent reports, proton Unlimited bundles Pass with Proton VPN, Proton Mail, Proton Drive, and more, including 500 GB of cloud storage. It’s the option to consider if you also want a VPN, encrypted email, and cloud storage alongside your password manager.

A password manager isn’t the most conspicuous Black Friday purchase, but it’s one you can put to work immediately: the next account you create, the next password you forget, or the next time a checkout asks for details you don’t have handy.

Proton’s offers are available to new people and include a 30-day money-back guarantee.

#69991. 11 career decisions high performers regret making too late

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

11 career decisions high performers regret making too late

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 28 min read (5614 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~28 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Some career decisions become costly only after too much time has passed.
  • Some career decisions become costly only after too much time has passed.
  • The single decision high performers almost always make too late is firing themselves from day-to-day fulfillment, because their ego is still addicted to being the hero inside the manufacturer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some career decisions become costly only after too much time has passed. The following insights, from experts in the field, reveal which moves high performers often wish they had made sooner, from protecting their health to asking for help and building stronger networks. These lessons offer clear steps for making better choices before regret sets in. Delegate Authority While Capacity Remains The single decision high performers almost always make too late is firing themselves from day-to-day fulfillment, because their ego is still addicted to being the hero inside the manufacturer. When I founded my first Scandinavian fine jewelry brand in Oslo at 22, I built our early momentum by personally touching every single bottleneck: approving every creative cut, negotiating every creator seeding deal, and rewriting campaign copy at 2:00 a.m. Because revenue was climbing and we were landing cultural placements like Khaby Lame and Vogue Scandinavia, I mistook exhaustion for leverage. The turning point came when I realized that by being the best operator in the room, I had capped the company’s valuation at the limit of my personal nervous system. High performers wait until they hit burnout to build standard operating procedures and delegate authority, whereas you actually have to hand off the keys while you still have 40% left in the tank. Once I forced myself to step out of daily order orchestration and document our visual and distribution protocols so the business ran without my fingerprints on every transaction, two things happened: Our enterprise value became transferable (allowing us to close a clean private acquisition exit in Q4 2024), and my own bandwidth opened up to direct film productions. If I could go back, I would have documented and delegated my favorite tasks 12 months earlier, not just the chores I hated. Mommi Live, founder, managing partner & creative director, Mommi Limited Archive Evidence Beyond External Platforms Keeping their track record inside someone else’s platform. High performers usually build their reputation where the work happens: an employer’s system, a marketplace profile, a client’s internal tools. It feels like the record will always be there. Then the job ends, the platform changes its rules, or the old proof simply stops being shown, and years of results are hard to point to. I learned this with my own business. I started selling video editing on Fiverr in 2020, while I was studying computer science. That grew into Mark Studios, which has completed more than 8,000 orders and earned 4,500+ reviews, with a 4.9 rating and Top Rated status. But Fiverr only shows roughly the last two years of reviews, so the visible proof of the early years keeps shrinking even as the total grows. The work was real. The evidence just lived somewhere I didn’t control. What I’d do differently, and what I tell anyone doing great work inside a company or a platform: Keep your own record from day one. Write a short case study after every project that matters, with the problem, what you did, and a measurable result. For a channel whose thumbnails and titles we’ve handled since August 2025, VidIQ highlighted views up 30.1% week over week when we captured the stats in May. That number now sits in a case study on my own website instead of only in a client conversation. Ask for testimonials you’re allowed to reuse, and save the numbers while they’re fresh. Your reputation is an asset. Make sure you hold a copy of it. Mark Santos, founder & creative director, Mark Studios LLC Ask for Help Before Depletion The decision I see high performers regret most isn’t burning out. It’s waiting until they’re depleted to ask for help, because by then the choice is already gone. Their body makes it for them. I’m a licensed counselor supervisor and president of a South Carolina practice with more than 60 therapists across 10 offices, plus online therapy. I watch this play out in my own field constantly. The strongest clinicians I supervise are usually the last ones to bring a hard case to supervision. Asking feels like admitting they can’t handle it, and they’ve built their whole identity around being the person others lean on. So they carry it quietly. And it doesn’t show up right away. It shows up months later as irritability, or dread on Sunday nights, or a sudden wish to quit work they used to love. What I tell them is pretty straightforward. Build the support in while things are still going well. Put a standing check-in on the calendar with a supervisor, a mentor, or a therapist before there’s anything urgent to report. When I started my practice with my husband, David, in 2019, I learned fast that the same logic applies to running a company. Support that you set up early costs you maybe an hour a week. Support that you set up late costs you a year of recovery. The best time to ask for help is when you don’t feel like you need it yet. Kenza Haddock, president, Oceanic Counseling Group Broadcast Accomplishments to Gain Advocacy High performers are great at getting things done, often to the detriment of their career progression. If you’re so busy taking care of things, then communicating out what you’re accomplishing is often the last thing on your list. That’s either because you don’t want to brag, or you assume others know what you’re working on. Not learning to communicate up and out is often a regret. I’ve worked with a senior leader whose manager was let go. They established relationships with their new manager and also with other senior leaders in the organization. They learned to communicate regularly as a part of their role to inform the what and the why of their accomplishments through one reorg after another. When yet another manager was let go, they were promoted into the role due to the awareness and extended support they’d built. I’m now working with a younger employee with a new manager on how to own their weekly reporting, proactively communicating to the team what their weekly accomplishments are and how these fit into the greater goals. People can only advocate for you if they can say what you actually do. High performers often learn this alternate side of their role far too late. Dana Zellers, executive & leadership coach, team facilitator, Dana Zellers Own Your Professional Future I’ve talked with more than a thousand executives in the past four years and the biggest regrets that I hear from high performers is relying on their employers to take care of them instead of taking ownership for their career decisions. I have had more clients than I can count who worked for Fortune 100 employers for 20+ years. They believed that they would retire with that company, but then the business changed, they lost their job, and they were left trying to figure out where to go next. No matter where you are in your career, you need to remember that companies are usually going to look out for themselves first. You need to plan your career accordingly. “Job hugging” has been the newest trend, where workers hang on to jobs that they don’t necessarily love. Sure, there is risk in leaving your job, but there is also risk at staying in your current job, especially if layoffs are on the horizon. Staying open to potential opportunities, both actively through networking and passively through an optimized LinkedIn profile, is key to building a career that lasts. Colleen Paulson, executive career consultant, Ageless Careers Align Ambition With Desired Work One decision high performers often make too late is to actively manage their careers rather than assuming that success in their current jobs will take care of that for them. Excelling at your job and managing your career are related, but they’re not the same thing. I’ve seen this play out in two ways. First, high performers become exceptionally good at identifying what it takes to succeed within their organizations. They earn promotions, navigate politics, and build expertise and relationships. But they don’t always stop to ask whether what they’re building is what they actually want. Over the last few years, I’ve worked with leaders who realized that the roles they’d spent years working toward had taken them further away from the work they loved, whether that’s working directly with clients or coaching their teams. We often think about the title and impact, but not the altitude we’ll have to lead at. A promotion often means moving away from doing the work yourself to creating the conditions for others to do it, through strategy, resource allocation, and management. That’s a very different job. Second, high performers forget to build career optionality before they need it. They invest heavily in building skills, relationships, and credibility within their organizations. That’s important, but incomplete. Internal recognition matters, but so does building an external professional network. Think of it as a savings account you’re contributing to over time. Too often, I’ve coached leaders who gave everything to their organizations, sometimes staying for more than a decade, only to find themselves facing a layoff, burnout, or a desire to pivot—and realizing they had limited external networks and little understanding of how their skills would translate elsewhere. A few simple ways to avoid these traps: • Before pursuing a promotion, talk to people already in the role. Understand what their day-to-day looks like, what they’ve had to give up, and what success actually requires. • While you’re happily employed, invest in relationships outside your organization and learn about other industries. Volunteer opportunities and nonprofit board service can be excellent ways to do this while also giving back. • The goal is not to constantly be on a job hunt. It’s to make sure you’re building a career that reflects what you want, with the flexibility to make different choices along the way. Lisa Friscia, president and founder, Franca Consulting Pursue Ventures Through Small Bets One decision high performers often regret making too late is waiting to act on an entrepreneurial idea because it feels safer to stay on secure footing. With more responsibility, high performers can get attached to income or get sucked into “golden handcuffs.” They’re less likely to leave for a more enjoyable job or take a risk at starting something up. I have seen this with seasoned corporate leaders who had a viable concept for years, but once they were settled with a mortgage, family responsibilities, and a stable role, the leap started to feel like too much to lose. The regret often sharpens when they later watch someone else succeed with a similar idea, because possibility suddenly looks like proof that they could have moved earlier. What could have been done differently is keeping the risk muscle active through small, regular bets while still employed, such as testing the idea in low-stakes ways and building comfort with uncertainty. That approach reduces the gap between the idea and bringing it to market, so the decision is not one big, intimidating jump. Also, it’s important to have accountability partners who ask us hard questions or challenge the status quo related to our experience, comfort, and career. How much money is enough? When is the right time? I hear high performers regret missed opportunities with a radical role departure or a job abroad or starting something new, going back to school when they were younger. We feel guilted or bullied into the norm by our families, peers, neighbors and society to do the “right” and “responsible” thing, then later wish we had taken the road less traveled or taken a risk. Janice Perkins, executive coach, Janice Perkins Restore Health Through Daily Habits The one decision high performers often regret is not focusing on their health and well-being as a function of improving their daily performance. All too often, high performers have had success all of their lives. They create habits in their 20s when their energy levels are high and their body can bounce back relatively quickly. As they start to advance their career in their 30s, 40s, and 50s, these high performers continue with these same habits, focusing only on work. Working late, missing sleep, skipping meals, and perhaps drinking alcohol (even in moderate amounts) drain more and more energy, physical and mental, from their daily output. To these habits, they add coffee to wake up and sugar intake to combat the energy crashes. This leads to poor sleep, and the cycle continues every day. It is possible to reverse these bad habits with small intentional changes in one’s daily lifestyle. A couple of simple examples are arising at the same time every day, including weekends, and getting morning daylight within the first 60-120 minutes of waking up. Steve Fiore, executive performance advisor, Rooted in Curiosity Serve Your Network Regularly As a career coach, I usually connect with high performers when they are in the midst of, or planning for, a transition. The #1 regret I hear is that leaders feel they lost touch with their network while building their careers. They understandably hesitate to make an ask when they haven’t connected in three, five, or even 10+ years. It can feel cringey and awkward reaching out when so much time has passed. But now more than ever, your network is your career net worth. So I hope more high achievers keep that in mind. The easiest way to keep in touch with your network? Be a helper. Haley McNeel Drake, résumé writer & career coach, The Career Revisory Exit Places That Diminish Your Worth One important decision I’ve seen time and time again among high performers is not leaving an organization sooner when their value went unrecognized. Being a high performer doesn’t automatically translate to timely promotions or special accolades for great work. In the pursuit of success, a high performer can work to increase their visibility and yet those efforts don’t lead to a promotion. Not because they’re doing anything wrong or focused on things that won’t get them noticed, but because of office politics or favoritism. What people often overlook and hate to admit is that you simply may be in the wrong environment where no matter what you do, your value will be unrecognized. For high performers, staying too long in an environment after making efforts to be “promotion ready” will eventually catch up, once they end up in an environment where they are valued, appreciated, and recognized for their work. Owning your competence, knowing your value, and being honest with yourself is part of high performance. Not getting a promotion the first time you ask for one isn’t necessarily a sign that you need to start looking or you’re being undervalued. However, the challenge arises when the same cycle repeats, and you’re getting empty promises instead of a kept word. Pay attention to nuance, yes: changes in the broader organization, natural attrition, etc. Timing is everything. But also, give yourself a timeline. If the opportunities you want to pursue don’t become available within that timeline, and those in charge can’t give you a blueprint to help you get where you want to be, you then make a different decision. And that could be planning your exit. Lisa De Nicola, leadership & executive coach; founder, HER Lead; Lisa De Nicola Broaden Expertise Outside Familiar Functions One decision high performers often make too late is stepping outside the area where they’ve already proven themselves. When you’re good at something, you tend to get more of it. You get promoted, take on bigger responsibilities, and become the person everyone relies on. That’s great for your career, but it can also keep you in a fairly narrow lane. Looking back, I would have sought out more of that exposure earlier rather than waiting for opportunities to come through my formal responsibilities. My advice to high performers is to take on something outside your comfort zone before you feel completely ready. Understanding how the whole business works prepares you for the next one. Thomas DeFabrizio, CFO, Vertage.

Some career decisions become costly only after too much time has passed. The following insights, from experts in the field, reveal which moves high performers often wish they had made sooner, from protecting their health to asking for help and building stronger networks. These lessons offer clear steps for making better choices before regret sets in.

The single decision high performers almost always make too late is firing themselves from day-to-day fulfillment, because their ego is still addicted to being the hero inside the manufacturer.

When I founded my first Scandinavian fine jewelry brand in Oslo at 22, I built our early momentum by personally touching every single bottleneck: approving every creative cut, negotiating every creator seeding deal, and rewriting campaign copy at 2:00 a.m. Because revenue was climbing and we were landing cultural placements like Khaby Lame and Vogue Scandinavia, I mistook exhaustion for leverage.

Industry observers note that the turning point came when I realized that by being the best operator in the room, I had capped the tech giant’s valuation at the limit of my personal nervous system. High performers wait until they hit burnout to build standard operating procedures and delegate authority, whereas you actually have to hand off the keys while you still have 40% left in the tank.

According to recent reports, once I forced myself to step out of daily order orchestration and document our visual and distribution protocols so the business ran without my fingerprints on every transaction, two things happened: Our enterprise value became transferable (allowing us to close a clean private acquisition exit in Q4 2024), and my own bandwidth opened up to direct film productions. If I could go back, I would have documented and delegated my favorite tasks 12 months earlier, not just the chores I hated.

Mommi Live, founder, managing partner & creative director, Mommi Limited.

Keeping their track record inside someone else’s platform.

High performers usually build their reputation where the work happens: an employer’s system, a marketplace profile, a client’s internal tools. It feels like the record will always be there. Then the job ends, the platform changes its rules, or the old proof simply stops being shown, and years of results are hard to point to.

Industry observers note that I learned this with my own business. I started selling video editing on Fiverr in 2020, while I was studying computer science. That grew into Mark Studios, which has completed more than 8,000 orders and earned 4,500+ reviews, with a 4.9 rating and Top Rated status. But Fiverr only reveals roughly the last two years of reviews, so the visible proof of the early years keeps shrinking even as the total grows. The work was real. The evidence just lived somewhere I didn’t control.

What I’d do differently, and what I tell anyone doing great work inside a organization or a platform: Keep your own record from day one. Write a short case study after every project that matters, with the problem, what you did, and a measurable result. For a channel whose thumbnails and titles we’ve handled since August 2025, VidIQ showed views up 30.1% week over week when we captured the stats in May. That number now sits in a case study on my own website instead of only in a client conversation. Ask for testimonials you’re allowed to reuse, and save the numbers while they’re fresh.

Your reputation is an asset. Make sure you hold a copy of it.

Mark Santos, founder & creative director, Mark Studios LLC.

Sources indicate that A good keyboard is essential to a good desk setup, and a Thunderbolt 5 dock makes that setup feel much cleaner. Keychron’s keyboards and latest dock are on sale with up to $48 off during the deal season.

I’ve been using a Keychron Q3 HE for quite some time now. Over the last year or two, I’ve made a lateral move to Gateron Dawn double-rail magnetic switches from the stock Nebula switches it came with. Now, Keychron sells a Q3 HE with improved hardware for an 8K polling rate and with Lime silent switches by default.

It’s an excellent keyboard, and my only complaint is that the white variant I have doesn’t exactly match my desk.

Sources indicate that most of Keychron’s deals are good right now, but the standout is the Thunderbolt 5 Dock, which was released earlier this year. I have mine plugged into my Mac Mini for the time being, but I use it on my Windows PC and Googlebook without glitch. The Thunderbolt 5 rating means it keeps up with next-gen speeds, but it’s backward-compatible and works with most devices. Just plug in a host device, and you have access to data and displays easily.

The Keychron Thunderbolt 5 Dock is down to $314, instead of $349. Considering it just debuted earlier in the year, now is a good time to get one if you’re looking for a docking option.

Right now, Keychron has a number of deals running that are worth checking out.

According to recent reports, the 8K Q3 HE magnetic keyboard from Keychron is down to $206 at 10% off. It was already a great deal for a fully aluminum case with good keycaps and excellent switches, but the new Black Friday deal sweetens the pot a little.

Industry observers note that the classic Q3 HE is no slouch, though. I’d recommend it in an instant, and it’s down to $191 instead of $239. That’s $48 down from the traditional price, and a much better deal than the 8K version if you don’t absolutely need the insanely high polling rate.

The K4 HE is another great option, and it’s a much friendlier $81 on Amazon. That’s down from the $115 it normally is. It’s another hall-effect (magnetic switch) keyboard, but with wood accents and in a smaller 60% layout.

Keychron’s deals won’t last into next month, ending on November 30.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI is changing how people choose between brands. And it’s moving from answering people’s questions to taking action on their behalf. Personal agents like Meta’s Muse take their cues from things like your email inbox and run with what they find. Now if that sounds scary, you’re behind the curve. More than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada started using Muse in its first six weeks. The number one thing they’re using it for? Shopping. And not just for significant purchases. In a McKinsey survey across 11 markets, nearly one-third (29%) of people who shop with artificial intelligence stated it was the strongest influence on their last purchase. Groceries are now the second most common thing people buy directly inside an AI tool, just behind clothes. Availability bias Historically, brands have grown on the back of a human shortcut called availability bias. When it comes to most everyday choices, the average person instinctively reaches for the brand that’s first to mind and first to find. AI behaves differently. It’s more literal than it is lazy, and the same is true whether it’s ChatGPT or a Grok Bot. It favors well-known brands when everything else is equal. In a recent study of AI skincare recommendations, the models picked the well-known brand every time when the products were identical. But give a lesser-known rival a rating that’s even less than a tenth of a star higher, and that stopped. Most of the time AI is prepared to compare, matching what a person wants against what a brand delivers. No wonder then that generative engine optimization (GEO), which means making sure your brand is the answer when someone asks AI, has become big business. And it works. BCG reports that a luxury fashion group fixed the structured data behind its website, and within eight weeks the rate at which AI search linked to its site had more than doubled. The problem is that it mostly works when you’re the only one doing it. In the skincare study, when every brand used the same technique, the gains all but canceled out, and brands that sat it out disappeared from the recommendations. GEO looks destined to become a cost of entry, not an advantage. A better way So, is there a better way? Rather than chasing the answer, what if a brand could shape the question people ask? Every choice has two sides: the person’s criteria and the brand’s attributes. A brand gets chosen when the two line up. GEO is about optimizing how a brand presents its attributes. What I’m suggesting is optimizing the criteria people bring. Marketing has a track record of changing what’s important to people. Brands can make things matter more than they’ve mattered before. Volvo, for example, made safety the way to judge a car. Nike did the same for cushioning in running shoes. Others changed how people judge. Dyson moved vacuums from suction power to suction that lasts. Avis moved car rentals from who’s biggest to who tries hardest. And some gave people something fresh to look for, as Head & Shoulders did with dandruff. Better still, frame the question around an attribute only you have. Ask AI for the best phone for FaceTime and there’s only one answer, and 88% of American teenagers already own an iPhone, according to a spring 2025 survey from Piper Sandler, the investment bank. In China, where people choose skincare by ingredient, L’Oréal’s Pro-Xylane became one of the most sought after, and only L’Oréal brands can use the name. Where do you start? Find the attribute you win on, relative to your size, and check that people and AI agree. If they disagree, shaping the question can backfire. If people believe something about your brand and AI doesn’t, you make the question matter and AI recommends a rival. If AI believes something about your brand and people don’t, AI recommends you, but nobody asks. Consider Dr. Whitney Bowe, the New York dermatologist who coined “skin cycling” on TikTok. She gave people a new question to ask, and retailers like Boots published guides on what to buy for it. Then she debuted her own brand, with a skin-cycling kit. She shaped the question, then built the brand to answer it. Maybe there are two new questions for every brief from here on out. What attribute do we win on? What question do we want people to ask?
